messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 73

**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 50-year-old married man of African descent who works as a plumber. He presents with a guarded posture, sitting on the edge of the chair, his large hands resting on his knees as if ready to stand. He speaks in a low, measured tone, often pausing to rub his face or stare at the floor. He has been married for 22 years and has three adult children.

The event that changed everything happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. Mr. A. was finishing a job at a commercial building in a part of the city he didn’t know well. He was packing his tools into the van when two young men approached him. One asked for the time. Before he could answer, the second man struck him from behind with a heavy object—later he learned it was a lead pipe. He remembers the sound more than the pain: a wet, hollow thud inside his skull. He fell to his knees, and they kicked him repeatedly, demanding his wallet, his phone, his watch. He remembers the weight of a boot on the back of his neck, pressing his face into the gravel. He remembers thinking, *I am going to die here. My wife will find me on the news.*

They left him bleeding, his ribs cracked, his left orbital bone fractured. A security guard found him twenty minutes later. He spent three days in the hospital.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. A. tried to return to normal. He told himself it was just a bad day, just a robbery, that he was lucky to be alive. But the world no longer felt solid. He stopped taking jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods. Then he stopped taking jobs that required him to park on the street. Then he stopped taking jobs that required him to work alone. Now, he has not worked in four months. His wife has taken on extra shifts at the hospital. He knows she is tired. He knows she is worried. But when she asks him what is wrong, he cannot find the words.

At night, he does not sleep. He lies awake, listening. Every creak of the house, every distant siren, every car door slamming—his body responds before his mind can catch up. His heart pounds. His palms sweat. He feels a cold dread rising from his stomach, as if the assault is happening again in the next room. When he does drift off, he dreams of the boot on his neck, of gravel grinding into his cheek. He wakes up gasping, sometimes shouting. His wife has started sleeping in the guest room.

During the day, he is hypervigilant. He cannot sit with his back to a door. In grocery stores, he scans every face, every pair of hands. He avoids crowds. He avoids eye contact with young men. He has stopped attending his church, where he used to sing in the choir. He tells himself he will go back next week. Next week never comes.

He feels a deep, gnawing shame. He was a man who fixed things. He was reliable. He was strong. Now he startles when his wife touches his shoulder. He cries in the bathroom, silently, so no one will hear. He has stopped answering his phone. His friends have stopped calling.

He does not know why he is here, in this office. His wife made the appointment. He says he is fine. He says he just needs to get back to work. But when he says this, his hands are shaking, and he will not meet my eyes. He is a man living in a world that no longer feels safe, haunted by a Tuesday afternoon he cannot leave behind.
